title: Haiti
capsule: The territory attested as Haiti between 1792 and 1803 corresponds to the revolutionary transformation of Saint-Domingue, France's most profitable Caribbean colony. In 1791 an enslaved uprising began; French commissioners abolished slavery in the northern province in August 1793 to secure Black military support, with the National Convention ratifying general emancipation in February 1794. Toussaint Louverture consolidated control of the island by 1801, promulgating a constitution that retained nominal French sovereignty while abolishing slavery permanently. Napoleon dispatched an expedition under Charles Leclerc in 1802 to reimpose metropolitan authority and restore slavery; Toussaint was seized by treachery in June 1802 and died in Fort de Joux in April 1803, but Jean-Jacques Dessalines continued the resistance and defeated the French at the Battle of Vertières on 18 November 1803, leading to independence declared on 1 January 1804.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The geographic extent of the revolutionary state covered the French colony of Saint-Domingue (western Hispaniola), which is well-defined cartographically; zones of effective control shifted continuously during the military campaigns and are only approximately mapped.
